idiom_name: kotlin.collections fold / foldRight / reduce / runningFold (Array, Iterable, Sequence)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library has the fold as a member of the collection hierarchy: fold(initial, operation) accumulates left to right and returns the initial value for an empty collection (declared for Array, the primitive arrays, Iterable and Sequence since Kotlin 1.0), foldRight applies the operation from the last element leftwards, reduce/reduceOrNull, foldIndexed and runningFold cover the no-seed, indexed and intermediate-accumulator cases, and Grouping.fold (1.1) folds each group of a groupingBy into a map. Prefer the monoid specializations (sum, sumOf, maxOrNull/minOrNull, joinToString) where they apply, and keep the stdlib fold for a custom algebra; a recursive data type gets the hand-written sealed/when catamorphism of the sibling variant, since the stdlib has no catamorphism for user types.
code_sketch:
val total = orders.fold(0L) { acc, o -> acc + o.amount }                 // left fold

val reversed = listOf(1, 2, 3).foldRight("") { v, acc -> "$acc$v" }      // right fold

val running = (1..5).runningFold(0) { acc, v -> acc + v }               // [0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15]

val same = orders.sumOf { it.amount.toLong() }                          // monoid specialization
pitfalls: reduce throws UnsupportedOperationException ("Empty collection can't be reduced") on an empty collection while fold returns the initial value: use reduceOrNull, or fold with an explicit identity, when empty input is possible.

Sequence folds are terminal and re-run the pipeline on every call: chaining several folds over the same sequence re-evaluates the source each time, and folding an unbounded sequence (generateSequence without a bound, sequence { }) never returns.

A fold that mutates a var captured from the enclosing scope instead of threading the accumulator is a lambda side effect: it breaks under sequence laziness (the lambda may run later or more than once) and cannot be reused as an algebra.

variants.name: Structural fold over a sealed hierarchy with an exhaustive when
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface + data-class cases + exhaustive when expression
variants.implementation_notes: The hand-written catamorphism is Kotlin's way to consume a recursive data type: declare the cases as data classes implementing a sealed interface, write one recursive function whose when expression switches over the cases, and let the compiler check exhaustiveness - sealed hierarchies restrict all direct subclasses to the same module and package, which is what lets the when be checked without an else clause. Use it for expression trees, state machines and protocol messages where the cases are data and the operations belong outside the type; keep the stdlib fold for homogeneous collections, where it is shorter and cheaper.
variants.code_sketch:
sealed interface Expr
data class Lit(val v: Int) : Expr
data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr
data class Mul(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr

fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) {          // no else: the compiler proves coverage
    is Lit -> e.v
    is Add -> eval(e.l) + eval(e.r)
    is Mul -> eval(e.l) * eval(e.r)
}
pitfalls: The exhaustiveness guarantee is only as good as recompilation: a when compiled against an older version of a sealed hierarchy gets a synthetic branch that throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException for a case added later, so sealed hierarchies that cross artifact boundaries need the same version discipline as any sealed API.

eval above is one stack frame per node and Kotlin does not optimize ordinary recursion (tailrec applies only to self-recursive tail calls, not to a fold that combines two children), so input-driven depth needs an explicit stack.

Data classes carry structural equals/hashCode/toString and are reference types: accumulating new data-class cases per step allocates, so fold into a mutable accumulator or a primitive carrier on hot paths.
